subtopics.title: Lorentz transformation equations
subtopics.theory_md:
The **Galilean** transformation $x'=x-vt$, $t'=t$ fails at speeds near $c$ because the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames (Einstein's second postulate; the first says the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames). Frame $S'$ moves with speed $v$ along $x$ relative to $S$ (origins coincide at $t=t'=0$):
$$x'=\gamma(x-vt),\quad y'=y,\quad z'=z,\quad t'=\gamma\left(t-\frac{vx}{c^2}\right),\quad \gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$$
Inverse: replace $v$ by $-v$ and swap primed and unprimed. For $v\ll c$, $\gamma\to1$ and Lorentz becomes Galilean.
subtopics.basics_md: Newton assumed time is the same for everyone. Experiments (Michelson-Morley) show light has the same speed for every observer, so space and time must mix. The factor $\gamma$ is 1 for everyday speeds and grows without limit as $v\to c$.
key_points: Postulates: laws same in all inertial frames; speed of light $c$ same in all inertial frames

State the two postulates of special relativity and write the Lorentz transformation equations for a frame $S'$ moving with speed $v$ along $x$ relative to $S$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Postulates**
1. The laws of physics have the same form in all inertial frames.
2. The speed of light in vacuum is $c$ in all inertial frames, independent of the motion of source or observer.

**Lorentz transformation** ($S'$ moves along $+x$ at speed $v$):
$$x'=\gamma(x-vt),\ y'=y,\ z'=z,\ t'=\gamma\left(t-\frac{vx}{c^2}\right),\ \gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$$
Inverse: $x=\gamma(x'+vt')$, $t=\gamma(t'+vx'/c^2)$.
points: Postulate 1: laws of physics same in all inertial frames
Postulate 2: speed of light same in all inertial frames

questions.q: Frame $S'$ moves at $0.6c$ along $x$ relative to $S$. An event occurs at $x=600$ m, $t=2\times10^{-6}$ s in $S$. Find $x'$ and $t'$ ($c=3\times10^8$ m/s).
Two spaceships leave Earth in the same direction at $0.8c$ and $0.9c$. Find the speed of the faster one as seen from the slower, using the relativistic velocity addition rule.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Rule** (velocity $u$ in $S$, $S'$ moving at $v$): $u'=\dfrac{u-v}{1-uv/c^2}$.

$u'=\dfrac{0.9c-0.8c}{1-(0.9)(0.8)}=\dfrac{0.1c}{1-0.72}=\dfrac{0.1c}{0.28}=0.357c\approx1.07\times10^8$ m/s

Galilean answer $0.1c$ is wrong; the result stays below $c$.

subtopics.title: Length contraction
subtopics.theory_md:
A rod at rest in $S'$ has **proper length** $L_0=x_2'-x_1'$. An observer in $S$ must record both ends at the **same instant** $t$ in $S$, so $t_2=t_1$ and
$$x_2'-x_1'=\gamma\left[(x_2-x_1)-v(t_2-t_1)\right]=\gamma L\ \Rightarrow\ L=L_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}$$
The length **along the motion** is contracted (Lorentz-FitzGerald contraction); lengths perpendicular to the motion are unchanged. Proper length is the longest. The effect is negligible for $v\ll c$.
subtopics.basics_md: Measuring a moving rod means marking where both ends are at one moment. Because moving observers disagree about 'one moment', the rod measures shorter, only along its direction of travel.
key_points: Proper length $L_0$ is measured in the frame where the rod is at rest
Ends must be noted simultaneously in the observer's frame ($\Delta t=0$)
Contraction only along the direction of motion

subtopics.title: Time dilation and its derivation
subtopics.theory_md:
**Proper time** $t_0$ is the interval between two events measured in the frame where both happen at the **same place**. In a frame where that clock moves at speed $v$, the interval is longer: a moving clock runs slow.

Derivation: in $S'$ two events at the same $x'$ have $t_0=t_2'-t_1'$. From $t=\gamma\left(t'+vx'/c^2\right)$ with $x_2'=x_1'$:
$$t_2-t_1=\gamma(t_2'-t_1')\ \Rightarrow\ t=\frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=\gamma t_0$$
Since $\gamma>1$, $t>t_0$. Evidence: cosmic-ray muons (rest lifetime 2.2 $\mu$s) reach the ground.
subtopics.basics_md: Imagine a clock that ticks by bouncing light between two mirrors. Seen from outside, the light must travel a longer diagonal path at the same speed $c$, so each tick takes longer. Same clock, slower to the outside observer.
key_points: Proper time: events at the same place in the clock's own frame
Muon lifetime extension is the experimental proof

questions.q: Why does time dilation not show up in everyday life? Give the experimental evidence that it is real.
questions.model_answer_md:
- For everyday speeds $v\ll c$, $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\approx1+v^2/2c^2$, which differs from 1 by about $10^{-12}$ even at jet speeds, so the effect is unmeasurable without atomic clocks.
- **Muon decay:** muons made in the upper atmosphere have rest lifetime $2.2\ \mu$s and would travel only about 660 m at nearly $c$, yet they reach the ground, because in the Earth frame their lifetime is $\gamma t_0$.
- Atomic clocks flown on aircraft also run slow by the predicted amount.
points: Muons reach the ground because lifetime is extended to $\gamma t_0$
Atomic clocks on aircraft confirm it

subtopics.title: Time dilation numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
Identify which time is **proper** (the clock travels with the event, so it is the shorter one) and apply $t=\gamma t_0$, with $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$.

Common types: time elapsed on Earth for a given ship time; the speed needed for a given dilation factor; distance covered by a fast particle before decay, $d=vt$ with the **dilated** $t$ (Earth frame); the same distance in the particle's own frame uses the contracted length and $t_0$, giving the same answer.
subtopics.basics_md: Always ask: whose clock sits at both events? That reading is $t_0$. The other observer measures a longer time. Never divide when you should multiply: the time on the moving clock is the smaller.
key_points: Proper time $t_0$ is the smaller reading
Write $v$ as a fraction of $c$ so $v^2/c^2$ is a pure number
Distance in the Earth frame is $v\,t$ with the dilated $t$

questions.q: Muons have proper mean lifetime $2\ \mu$s. A beam moves at $0.8c$. Find the lifetime in the lab and the average distance travelled before decay, and compare with the classical value.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-0.64}}=1.667$

Lab lifetime $t=\gamma t_0=1.667\times2=3.33\ \mu$s

Distance $d=vt=0.8\times3\times10^8\times3.33\times10^{-6}=800$ m

Classical (no dilation): $d_0=vt_0=0.8\times3\times10^8\times2\times10^{-6}=480$ m.

**Result:** 3.33 $\mu$s and 800 m, against 480 m classically.
points: Classical value 480 m, so dilation increases the range

subtopics.title: Variation of mass with velocity
subtopics.theory_md:
Relativistic mass of a particle of rest mass $m_0$ moving at speed $v$:
$$m=\frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=\gamma m_0$$
Mass rises with speed and tends to infinity as $v\to c$, so no particle with rest mass can reach $c$. It is the relativistic form of momentum, $p=mv=\gamma m_0v$, that keeps momentum conserved in every inertial frame. For $v\ll c$, $m\approx m_0$.
subtopics.basics_md: The faster something goes, the harder it is to speed up further. Relativity records this as growing mass: the push you give adds energy, and energy has mass. At $0.6c$ the mass is already 1.25 times the rest mass.
key_points: $m\to\infty$ as $v\to c$, so $c$ is the speed limit for matter
$m_0$ is rest mass, same in all frames

questions.q: As the speed of a particle approaches $c$, its relativistic mass
At what speed is the mass of a particle double its rest mass? What is the mass at $0.6c$?
State how mass varies with velocity and explain why a particle with non-zero rest mass cannot reach the speed of light.
questions.model_answer_md:
$m=\dfrac{m_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$, where $m_0$ is the rest mass.

As $v\to c$, $\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\to0$ so $m\to\infty$: the energy $mc^2$ needed to accelerate it grows without limit. Hence $c$ is the upper speed limit for matter.
points: Infinite energy needed, so $c$ cannot be reached

subtopics.title: Mass-energy equivalence, E = mc^2
subtopics.theory_md:
Work done raises kinetic energy: $dK=F\,dx=v\,d(mv)=mv\,dv+v^2dm$. Differentiating $m^2(c^2-v^2)=m_0^2c^2$ gives $c^2dm=v^2dm+mv\,dv$, so $dK=c^2dm$. Integrating from $m_0$ to $m$:
$$K=(m-m_0)c^2,\qquad E=K+m_0c^2=mc^2$$
Rest energy $E_0=m_0c^2$. A mass change $\Delta m$ releases or needs $\Delta E=\Delta m\,c^2$. For electrons, $m_0c^2=0.511$ MeV; $1$ eV $=1.6\times10^{-19}$ J.
subtopics.basics_md: Energy has inertia. Adding kinetic energy adds mass in the ratio $1/c^2$, and even a body at rest holds energy $m_0c^2$. Because $c^2$ is huge, a tiny mass is a vast energy.

questions.why: Total energy $mc^2$ minus rest energy $m_0c^2$; $\tfrac12m_0v^2$ is the low-speed limit.

questions.q: How much energy is equivalent to 1 mg of mass? ($c=3\times10^8$ m/s)
Find the kinetic energy of an electron moving at $0.8c$ (rest energy 0.511 MeV). Compare it with the classical $\tfrac12m_0v^2$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-0.64}}=1.667$

Relativistic: $K=(\gamma-1)m_0c^2=0.667\times0.511=0.341$ MeV

Classical: $\tfrac12m_0c^2(0.8)^2=0.5\times0.511\times0.64=0.164$ MeV

**Result:** $K=0.341$ MeV, about twice the classical 0.164 MeV, so the classical formula fails near $c$.
points: Classical value 0.164 MeV, relativistic is about twice
